Jada
JAY-dah
n. (proper name; a Jerahmeelite, son of Onam)
Hebrew Yada', knowing, wise, from yada', to know.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jada is a descendant of Jerahmeel of Judah, the son of Onam. “Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam” (1 Chronicles 2:26). “And the sons of Onam were, Shammai, and Jada. And the sons of Shammai; Nadab, and Abishur” (1 Chronicles 2:28). “And the sons of Jada the brother of Shammai; Jether, and Jonathan: and Jether died without children” (1 Chronicles 2:32). His line continued through Jonathan, the father of Peleth and Zaza. The genealogy notes two men who died childless, Seled and Jether, and in each case shows how the line went on another way. Jada's name means knowing. The God who knows His own preserved the house of Jada through the one son who had children, and the Chronicler recorded both the loss and the continuance.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Jada is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Jada is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

The name appears in 1 Chronicles 2:28 and 2:32.

He was a son of Onam, son of Jerahmeel.

His sons were Jether and Jonathan.

The name means knowing.

Key Scripture

1Ch 2:26 — "Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam."

1Ch 2:28 — "And the sons of Onam were, Shammai, and Jada. And the sons of Shammai; Nadab, and Abishur."

1Ch 2:30 — "And the sons of Nadab; Seled, and Appaim: but Seled died without children."

1Ch 2:32 — "And the sons of Jada the brother of Shammai; Jether, and Jonathan: and Jether died without children."

Modern Corruption

A childless death is treated as the end of a name; Jada's house continued through Jonathan when Jether died without children.

expand to see more

Modern readers skim 1 Chronicles 2 and 4 as lists without meaning. They are the register of the royal tribe, and their small notes of grace, a servant adopted as heir, a prayer answered, a craftsman named, are placed there on purpose.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genealogies of Judah are the line out of which the Lion of the tribe of Judah came. The Chronicler wrote them for a people back from exile, to show that God had kept the families of the promise.
